subject: Biology
title: Fungal Diseases
description: A quick, practical guide to Fungal Diseases.

hook.text: Fungi cause infections ranging from mild athlete's foot to life-threatening lung disease.

buildup.text: Candida yeast lives harmlessly in your body but causes thrush when the immune system weakens.

discovery.text: Aspergillus mold spores float in the air. Healthy lungs clear them, but weakened lungs can't.

twist.text: Fungal infections kill about 1.5 million people a year—more than malaria.

climax.text: Antifungal drugs are limited, and resistant fungi like Candida auris are spreading in hospitals.

punchline.text: Fungi are quiet killers hiding in plain air.

quiz.question: How many people do fungal infections kill each year?

details.summary: Fungal infections range from common skin conditions like athlete's foot to life-threatening systemic infections in immunocompromised patients. Fungi like Candida, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus cause over 1.5 million deaths annually, a toll largely unrecognized by the global health community.
details.whyItMatters: Fungal diseases kill more people than malaria yet receive far less funding and attention. Rising antifungal resistance and increasing immunocompromised populations from HIV and immunosuppressive therapies make this a growing crisis.
takeaways: Fungal infections kill over 1.5 million people annually worldwide
Only four classes of antifungal drugs exist compared to dozens of antibiotics
Climate change may select for heat-tolerant fungi able to infect warm-blooded hosts

faq.question: Why are fungal infections so difficult to treat?
faq.answer: Fungi are eukaryotes like human cells, so drugs that kill fungi often damage human cells too. Only four classes of antifungals exist. Treatment courses are long, often months. Resistance is growing, especially in Candida auris, which resists all major drug classes.

faq.question: Why might climate change increase fungal infections?
faq.answer: Our high body temperature protects us from most environmental fungi. As global temperatures rise, fungi may adapt to higher temperatures, breaching this thermal barrier. Candida auris emerged simultaneously on three continents, possibly driven by warming environments.
